request: How much do rich countries spend on health, and does spending more buy longer lives? #interactive

spec.title: Does more health spending buy longer lives?

sources.title: Health at a Glance 2023
sources.finding: spending per person and life expectancy, about 2022

elements.details: A saturating curve drawn by eye through the points, $y \approx 84 - 18e^{-x/1400}$: steep below about \$3,000 a head, nearly flat above \$5,000. It is a reading of the pattern, not a causal estimate.
United States, about 2022: roughly \$12,500 per person per year (purchasing-power adjusted), life expectancy at birth about 77 years.

elements.text: Steep, then flat: how, not how much

card.title: Does more health spending buy longer lives?

commands.speak: How much do rich countries spend on health, and does more money buy longer lives?

ask.question: Start with a guess, not a test: how much does America spend on health, per person, each year?
ask.wrong: You said {g}. The real figure is about {g.true}, off by {g.off}. Most people guess far lower.

commands.speak: About twelve and a half thousand dollars, for every man, woman and child.
The typical rich country spends around five thousand, less than half as much.
So you'd expect Americans to buy the longest lives on earth.
Mexico spends about twelve hundred dollars a head, and lives to about seventy-five.
Spain spends under four and a half thousand, and reaches eighty-three.
Japan and Britain spend around five thousand, and land at eighty-four and eighty-one.
Switzerland and Germany spend about eight thousand…
…and buy no more years than Japan.
Join them, and the curve climbs fast,
then goes almost flat.
Where the curve has levelled off, twelve and a half thousand should mean at least eighty-four years.

ask.question: Now guess: does an American live longer or shorter than someone in Japan, Germany, or Mexico?
ask.right: You got {g} of 3. America beats only Mexico.
ask.wrong: You got {g} of 3. Most people rank America higher than it is.

commands.speak: The real point lands at about seventy-seven years.
That's roughly seven years below where the money says it should be.
Where does the money go?
Partly into prices: Americans pay far more for the same drugs, scans and doctor visits.
Partly against deaths medicine reaches too late for, like overdoses, shootings, car crashes and obesity.
This is a correlation, not an experiment: wealth, diet and safety move both axes at once.
Explore: click any country to read its numbers, and look at how little height the curve gains past five thousand dollars.
Up to a few thousand dollars a head, money buys years fast;
beyond that, what you buy and how people live matter far more than how much you spend.

quiz.question: Two countries each add $1,000 per person to health. A spends $2,000 and lives to 74; B spends $9,000 and lives to 82. Where will the extra $1,000 most likely buy more years?
quiz.right: Country A: at $2,000 the curve is still steep, so $1,000 climbs far; at $9,000 it is almost flat.
quiz.wrong: Find each country's spending on the curve. Is the curve steep or flat there? The same $1,000 climbs much further where the curve is steep.
